Frame Materials, Colours, and Proportions for Contemporary Pieces

Once you have settled on a style direction, the next decisions are about material, colour and frame width. These choices work together and getting the proportions wrong is one of the most common framing mistakes I see.

[[IMG|frame-materials-colours-proportions|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Frame Width vs Artwork Size". Then a clear VISUAL comparison showing three simple labelled rectangles side by side: a small artwork with a thin frame labelled "Small artwork: narrow frame (1–2cm)"; a medium artwork with a medium frame labelled "Medium artwork: medium frame (2–4cm)"; and a large artwork with a wider frame labelled "Large artwork: wider frame (4–6cm+)". Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Frame Material Options at a Glance

Material Best For Feel / Finish Durability
Natural wood (oak, pine, walnut) Warm, organic, Scandi or Japandi interiors Tactile, warm Very good
Painted wood (white, black, grey) Most contemporary styles Clean, versatile Very good
Aluminium / metal Photography, graphic prints, industrial interiors Sleek, modern Excellent
Acrylic / perspex face mount Photography and digital prints Ultra-modern, immersive Good
Gilded or painted ornate wood Deliberate contrast with raw/abstract art Dramatic, gallery-feel Good

For proportions, a rough guide I always use: the frame profile (width) should be no more than about 10% of the artwork's shorter dimension. So for a 50cm-wide piece, a frame no wider than about 5cm looks balanced. Go wider than that and the frame starts to dominate.

Pro Tip: Hold a length of card or tape against your artwork to simulate a frame width before you buy anything. It takes two minutes and saves a lot of regret later.

How Frame Colour Affects the Mood and Perception of Contemporary Art

Colour is where framing gets genuinely interesting — and where I see people make surprisingly emotional decisions. The frame colour you pick will change how the artwork reads, sometimes dramatically.

[[IMG|frame-colour-mood-perception|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — mirrors, wall-mounted shelves, sconces. A wide, clean hallway with smooth plaster walls painted in a warm off-white. On a slim console table sit four flat picture frames in different colours — matte black, natural oak, white, and brushed gold — arranged side by side as if being considered. Small ceramic decorative objects are placed between the frames. A South Asian woman in her late twenties, wearing a rust-coloured linen shirt and jeans, stands at the console comparing the frames, holding one up thoughtfully.]]

Frame Colour Guide for Contemporary Artwork

  • Black — sharpens contrast, adds drama, works brilliantly with bold graphic art, monochrome photography, or high-saturation paintings. It is also incredibly versatile across interior styles.
  • White or off-white — airy and gallery-like, lifts lighter colour palettes, and suits pastel or watercolour-style contemporary work very well.
  • Natural wood tones — warm, grounding, and brilliant for earthy abstract work or organic contemporary prints. They bring a humanising quality to rooms that can otherwise feel cold.
  • Gold or brass — creates a luxe feel, works beautifully as a contrast to raw or textural contemporary pieces, and adds warmth without the visual weight of dark wood.
  • Grey or charcoal — subtle and sophisticated, ideal if you want the frame to recede and the colour in the art to speak fully.
  • Coloured frames — a deep navy, forest green, or terracotta frame can be brilliant when it picks up a secondary colour in the art. Use sparingly and with intention.

Here's something I always tell clients: if you are unsure, pick a colour that appears in the artwork but is NOT the dominant colour. So if your abstract has a big swathe of burnt orange with small marks of teal, a teal-toned frame is a brilliant quiet nod to the piece without shouting.

Real Example: A client of mine had a large botanical print with deep greens and cream tones. She wanted a gold frame but worried it would look too traditional. We went for a slim brushed-brass profile — barely 2cm wide — and it was perfect. The warmth of the metal brought out the golden undertones in the cream without making it feel dated.

Mounts, Glazing, and Other Framing Components

This is the section most beginners skip, and it is genuinely where good framing happens. The mount (also called a mat or passepartout) and the glazing can make or break how your artwork looks — and how well it survives long-term.

[[IMG|mounts-glazing-framing-components|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Anatomy of a Picture Frame". Then a clear VISUAL diagram showing a labelled cross-section of a framed picture — with labelled arrows pointing to each component: "Frame (moulding)", "Mount / Mat", "Glazing (glass or acrylic)", "Backing board", "Artwork". Minimal words, generous white space, simple clean illustration style, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

What Each Component Does

  • Mount / mat: A border of card between the artwork and the frame. It creates visual breathing space and keeps the art from touching the glazing (which causes damage over time). For contemporary work, an oversized mount — wider than you think looks right — often looks most striking.
  • Conservation-grade mount board: If your artwork is a print or original on paper, always use acid-free, conservation-grade mount board. Acidic board will yellow and damage artwork over time.
  • Standard float glass: The cheapest option and fine for rooms away from direct light.
  • Non-reflective / anti-reflection glass: Reduces glare, great for well-lit rooms, but can slightly soften the image — worth testing before committing.
  • UV-protective glass or acrylic: A must for any artwork you care about, especially in rooms with strong natural light. It blocks UV rays that fade pigments.
  • Museum / conservation glass: The best you can get — UV protection and near-invisible anti-reflection coating. Worth the investment for original pieces.
  • Backing board: Seals the back of the frame to keep dust and moisture out. Should also be acid-free for paper works.
Pro Tip: For canvas works, you do not need glazing at all — canvas is designed to be displayed open to the air. Adding glass to a canvas is both unnecessary and can actually encourage moisture build-up behind it.

Step-by-Step DIY Framing Instructions for Contemporary Art

Right, let's get practical. DIY framing is absolutely achievable for most contemporary artworks, especially prints and paper-based pieces. Here is exactly how I approach it.

[[IMG|diy-framing-instructions-contemporary-art|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — a floating shelf, a small mirror. A bright, organised kitchen table being used as a DIY framing workspace. On the table: a clean wooden frame broken down into pieces, a white mount board cut to size, a ruler, a bone folder, a roll of brown self-adhesive framing tape, white cotton gloves, a pencil, and a small spirit level. Everything is laid out neatly on a sheet of clean kraft paper. A mixed-race man in his mid-thirties, wearing a relaxed grey T-shirt, carefully positions a print onto the mount board with gloved hands, concentrating on the alignment.]]

Step-by-Step: How to Frame a Contemporary Art Print at Home

  • Step 1 — Measure the artwork: Measure the visible image area precisely. If it is a print with a white border, decide whether you want to show the border or crop it with the mount. Note the dimensions down.
  • Step 2 — Choose and cut the mount: Buy conservation-grade mount board from an art supply shop. Cut the aperture slightly smaller than the image (typically 3–4mm smaller on each side) so the artwork sits neatly behind it. A mount cutter gives you a clean 45-degree bevel — well worth the investment if you frame regularly.
  • Step 3 — Hinge the artwork: Use Japanese tissue tape (acid-free, reversible) to attach the artwork to the backing board with two T-hinges at the top. Never use regular sticky tape or masking tape — these will damage the artwork.
  • Step 4 — Clean the glazing: Clean both sides of the glass or acrylic thoroughly with a lint-free cloth before assembling. Even a small smudge will be visible once it is framed and hanging.
  • Step 5 — Assemble the frame: Lay the frame face-down on a soft surface. Place the glazing in first, then the mount, then the artwork on its backing board. Check the front before closing — flip it briefly to spot any dust trapped inside.
  • Step 6 — Secure the backing: Use frame points or flexible tabs to hold the backing board in place. Run self-adhesive brown framing tape around the back join to seal against dust.
  • Step 7 — Fit the hanging hardware: Attach two D-ring hangers (not the single central clip that usually comes in cheap frames) and thread picture wire through them. This two-point system gives far more stability on the wall.
  • Step 8 — Hang it level: Use a spirit level. Always. Even pieces that look "nearly level" will bother you every day.
Pro Tip: If you are working with acrylic glazing rather than glass, remove the protective film only at the very last moment before assembly — static builds up on acrylic and attracts dust like a magnet.

How to Frame Canvas vs Paper vs Print Contemporary Art

Not all contemporary art is created equal when it comes to framing — the medium makes a real difference to the approach. Let me break this down by type because the rules genuinely vary.

[[IMG|frame-canvas-paper-print-contemporary-art|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Framing by Medium". Then three clearly labelled vertical columns side by side, each with a simple icon at the top representing the medium: a stretched canvas icon labelled "Canvas", a sheet of paper icon labelled "Paper / Original", and a printed sheet icon labelled "Art Print / Giclée". Below each icon, list 3 short bullet points describing the framing approach for that medium. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Medium-by-Medium Framing Guide

  • Stretched canvas: No glazing needed. Use a floater frame — this sits around the canvas with a small gap so the edges of the painting remain visible. Choose a frame depth that matches your canvas depth (check this before buying). Canvas does not need a mount.
  • Unstretched / rolled canvas: Either stretch it yourself onto a wooden stretcher frame first, or take it to a professional framer. Do not frame it flat without stretching — it will wrinkle and sag.
  • Watercolour, gouache, or original on paper: Always use conservation-grade materials throughout. Hinge the artwork (do not dry-mount or glue it). Use UV-protective glazing. A generous mount helps protect the paper and creates a beautiful gallery feel.
  • Giclée or archival art print: Treat like paper — acid-free mount, UV glazing, hinge hanging. Avoid dry-mounting unless you do not mind it being permanent (dry-mounting bonds the print to a board and cannot be reversed).
  • Poster or non-archival print: Standard framing is fine here since archival longevity is less of a concern. A simple clip frame or standard frame with float glass works well.
  • Mixed media / textured pieces: Use a box frame or spacer bars to create depth between the artwork surface and the glazing. This protects raised elements and gives the piece room to be itself.

I had a client bring me a beautiful large watercolour she had bought on holiday in the Lake District. She had taken it to a cheap framing service that dry-mounted it — permanently bonded it to a backing board with no reversibility. If she had ever wanted to reframe it or sell it, the damage would have been irreversible. Always ask a framer whether they use reversible mounting methods for original art.

[[PRODUCT|large format wall art prints on canvas]]

Digital and Photographic Contemporary Art Framing Considerations

Photographic and digital art has its own framing language, and it is one of the fastest-growing categories of contemporary work people bring home. The good news is you have some genuinely exciting options beyond the standard frame-and-glass approach.

[[IMG|digital-photographic-contemporary-art-framing|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — a slim wall-mounted shelf, wall-mounted light sconce, a round mirror. A sleek, modern home office or study with a plaster-effect feature wall in pale clay. A large slim aluminium picture frame leans against the wall on a credenza, face forward, its glossy surface reflecting soft morning light. Next to it on the credenza sit a tall ceramic lamp, a small succulent plant, and a stack of design books. A dark-skinned African woman in her early forties, dressed in a smart navy blazer, stands to one side of the credenza examining the slim metal frame with interested focus.]]

Framing Options for Photography and Digital Art

  • Slim aluminium frames: Clean, industrial, and brilliant for black-and-white or high-contrast photography. They put all the focus on the image.
  • Acrylic face mount (diasec): The print is face-bonded to a thick acrylic sheet. The result is immersive, jewel-like depth. Very popular in contemporary photography and digital art. No frame required — wall-mounted directly via standoffs.
  • Aluminium dibond print: The image is printed directly onto a thin aluminium composite panel. Incredibly durable, completely flat, and can be hung without a frame for a very modern look.
  • Metal prints: Dye-sublimation printing onto aluminium gives vivid, high-contrast results. Floats off the wall slightly and needs no frame.
  • Canvas print: Digital or photographic images printed onto canvas, then stretched. A classic option but be aware that very fine detail can appear slightly softer on canvas texture.

Common Framing Mistakes to Avoid with Contemporary Artwork

I have seen a lot of beautifully framed artwork over the years — and equally, a lot of framing that did the art no favours at all. Here are the mistakes I see most often, and exactly how to avoid them.

Top Framing Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)

  • Choosing a frame that is too heavy: A wide, ornate frame overpowers contemporary work 90% of the time. Go slimmer than your instinct — you can always adjust, but you cannot unspend money on a frame that overwhelms the art.
  • Skipping the mount: Particularly common with prints. The mount is not just decorative — it physically keeps the artwork from touching the glass (which causes moisture damage and sticking). Always use one for paper-based works.
  • Using regular sticky tape to attach artwork: This is one I still see all the time. Regular tape is acidic, turns yellow, and will permanently damage anything it touches. Use Japanese tissue tape or conservation-grade hinging tape only.
  • Dry-mounting originals: As I mentioned, dry-mounting is permanent. It devalues original artwork and prevents reframing. Only do this for inexpensive prints you are absolutely certain will never be reframed.
  • Hanging with a single central hook: Even with a hanging wire across the back, a single central hook allows the frame to pivot and tilt over time. Use two hooks set apart, lined up with the D-rings on the frame back.
  • Not cleaning the glazing before assembly: One fingerprint trapped inside the frame under the glass will bother you for years. Spend two minutes cleaning both sides properly before you close it up.
  • Hanging too high: The standard rule is that the centre of the artwork sits at approximately eye level — roughly 145–150cm from the floor. Most people hang artwork too high, which makes the room feel disconnected.
  • Matching the frame colour to the wall colour exactly: This makes the frame disappear and can make the artwork look unanchored. A slight contrast — even subtle — gives the piece its own presence.

More About Getting Framing Right

Framing is genuinely one of those skills where a little knowledge goes a long way — and the gap between a competently framed piece and a poorly framed one is far more visible than most people expect.

One thing worth knowing is that the art world has thought carefully about this for a long time. If you want to go deeper on the theory side, this guide from Artsy — 5 Tips for Finding the Right Frame for Your Art — is a genuinely useful read from people who think about this professionally every day.

What I would add to the practical side is this: trust the artwork. Contemporary art is made by people who thought hard about colour, form and composition. Your job as the framer is to present it — not to interpret it or add to it.

When in doubt, go simpler. A plain, well-proportioned frame in a neutral colour will never embarrass you. It is the overcomplicated, over-matched, over-decorated frame that almost always dates and disappoints.

Ready to Frame Your Contemporary Art?

Framing contemporary art is really about one thing: giving the work the best possible chance to be itself in your space. You do not need to be a professional framer or spend a fortune to do that well.

Start with the medium — know whether your piece is canvas, paper, or a print, because that shapes every other decision. Then think about the frame as a quiet supporting player, not a star. Choose materials and colours that complement without competing, use the right components, and take your time with the assembly if you are doing it yourself.

The difference a well-chosen frame makes is genuinely remarkable. I have watched pieces that seemed unremarkable on first viewing completely come alive once they were properly framed and hung at the right height. It is one of my favourite things to see in a client's home.

Knowing how to frame contemporary art is one of the most satisfying things you can do for your home — get it right and a single piece can transform an entire room. The good news is that it is absolutely something you can do yourself, even if you have never picked up a mount cutter in your life. This guide walks you through every step, from choosing the right frame style to hanging the finished piece on your wall.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in front of a beautiful piece of wall art and felt completely stumped about how to frame it without ruining what makes it so special?

Quick answer: To frame contemporary art well, choose a clean, minimal frame in a material and colour that complements rather than competes with the piece. Use a generous mount if the work is on paper, select UV-protective glazing, and match the frame's proportions to the artwork's scale. DIY framing is very achievable with the right tools and a bit of patience.

Contemporary art covers a huge range of styles — abstract paintings, bold graphic prints, photographic works, mixed-media pieces and more. What they tend to share is a visual energy that deserves a frame that works with it, not against it. Whether you are shopping for unique wall art or already have a piece on your hands, framing is the step that makes it look truly finished. The same goes for broader unique home decor — the way you present things matters just as much as the things themselves.

Choosing the Right Frame Style for Contemporary Art

The frame style you choose sends an immediate visual signal, so it is worth thinking about this before anything else. Contemporary art generally calls for either a minimalist frame that stays out of the way, or a carefully chosen traditional frame that creates a deliberate contrast.

Minimalist vs Traditional Frames: Which Suits Contemporary Art?

  • Minimalist frames (thin profiles, clean lines, metal or plain wood) let the artwork lead — ideal for abstract work, bold colour-field pieces, and photography.
  • Floater frames give canvas work the illusion of floating in mid-air, which suits contemporary painting beautifully.
  • Traditional ornate frames can work brilliantly with contemporary art as a deliberate juxtaposition — a heavy gold frame around a raw abstract can feel very intentional and gallery-like.
  • Box frames work well for mixed-media or textured pieces that need a little depth between the art and the glazing.
  • Avoid frames with lots of decorative carving unless you specifically want the contrast effect — they can visually compete with bold contemporary work.

I once helped a client who had a stunning large-format abstract in rich terracotta and ochre tones. Her instinct was to find a frame that matched those warm colours exactly. We tried it — and honestly, it looked fussy and crowded. The moment we switched to a slim natural oak floater frame, the painting breathed. The rule I always come back to is: the frame should hold the artwork, not join it.

Pro Tip: Visit a local gallery and look at how they hang contemporary work — most use very thin, simple frames or no frames at all on canvas. That restraint is not laziness; it is a deliberate choice to keep attention on the art.

How Frame Colour Affects the Mood and Perception of Contemporary Art

Colour is where framing gets genuinely interesting — and where I see people make surprisingly emotional decisions. The frame colour you pick will change how the artwork reads, sometimes dramatically.

Frame Colour Guide for Contemporary Artwork

  • Black — sharpens contrast, adds drama, works brilliantly with bold graphic art, monochrome photography, or high-saturation paintings. It is also incredibly versatile across interior styles.
  • White or off-white — airy and gallery-like, lifts lighter colour palettes, and suits pastel or watercolour-style contemporary work very well.
  • Natural wood tones — warm, grounding, and brilliant for earthy abstract work or organic contemporary prints. They bring a humanising quality to rooms that can otherwise feel cold.
  • Gold or brass — creates a luxe feel, works beautifully as a contrast to raw or textural contemporary pieces, and adds warmth without the visual weight of dark wood.
  • Grey or charcoal — subtle and sophisticated, ideal if you want the frame to recede and the colour in the art to speak fully.
  • Coloured frames — a deep navy, forest green, or terracotta frame can be brilliant when it picks up a secondary colour in the art. Use sparingly and with intention.

Here's something I always tell clients: if you are unsure, pick a colour that appears in the artwork but is NOT the dominant colour. So if your abstract has a big swathe of burnt orange with small marks of teal, a teal-toned frame is a brilliant quiet nod to the piece without shouting.

Real Example: A client of mine had a large botanical print with deep greens and cream tones. She wanted a gold frame but worried it would look too traditional. We went for a slim brushed-brass profile — barely 2cm wide — and it was perfect. The warmth of the metal brought out the golden undertones in the cream without making it feel dated.

Mounts, Glazing, and Other Framing Components

This is the section most beginners skip, and it is genuinely where good framing happens. The mount (also called a mat or passepartout) and the glazing can make or break how your artwork looks — and how well it survives long-term.

What Each Component Does

  • Mount / mat: A border of card between the artwork and the frame. It creates visual breathing space and keeps the art from touching the glazing (which causes damage over time). For contemporary work, an oversized mount — wider than you think looks right — often looks most striking.
  • Conservation-grade mount board: If your artwork is a print or original on paper, always use acid-free, conservation-grade mount board. Acidic board will yellow and damage artwork over time.
  • Standard float glass: The cheapest option and fine for rooms away from direct light.
  • Non-reflective / anti-reflection glass: Reduces glare, great for well-lit rooms, but can slightly soften the image — worth testing before committing.
  • UV-protective glass or acrylic: A must for any artwork you care about, especially in rooms with strong natural light. It blocks UV rays that fade pigments.
  • Museum / conservation glass: The best you can get — UV protection and near-invisible anti-reflection coating. Worth the investment for original pieces.
  • Backing board: Seals the back of the frame to keep dust and moisture out. Should also be acid-free for paper works.
Pro Tip: For canvas works, you do not need glazing at all — canvas is designed to be displayed open to the air. Adding glass to a canvas is both unnecessary and can actually encourage moisture build-up behind it.

Step-by-Step DIY Framing Instructions for Contemporary Art

Right, let's get practical. DIY framing is absolutely achievable for most contemporary artworks, especially prints and paper-based pieces. Here is exactly how I approach it.

Step-by-Step: How to Frame a Contemporary Art Print at Home

  • Step 1 — Measure the artwork: Measure the visible image area precisely. If it is a print with a white border, decide whether you want to show the border or crop it with the mount. Note the dimensions down.
  • Step 2 — Choose and cut the mount: Buy conservation-grade mount board from an art supply shop. Cut the aperture slightly smaller than the image (typically 3–4mm smaller on each side) so the artwork sits neatly behind it. A mount cutter gives you a clean 45-degree bevel — well worth the investment if you frame regularly.
  • Step 3 — Hinge the artwork: Use Japanese tissue tape (acid-free, reversible) to attach the artwork to the backing board with two T-hinges at the top. Never use regular sticky tape or masking tape — these will damage the artwork.
  • Step 4 — Clean the glazing: Clean both sides of the glass or acrylic thoroughly with a lint-free cloth before assembling. Even a small smudge will be visible once it is framed and hanging.
  • Step 5 — Assemble the frame: Lay the frame face-down on a soft surface. Place the glazing in first, then the mount, then the artwork on its backing board. Check the front before closing — flip it briefly to spot any dust trapped inside.
  • Step 6 — Secure the backing: Use frame points or flexible tabs to hold the backing board in place. Run self-adhesive brown framing tape around the back join to seal against dust.
  • Step 7 — Fit the hanging hardware: Attach two D-ring hangers (not the single central clip that usually comes in cheap frames) and thread picture wire through them. This two-point system gives far more stability on the wall.
  • Step 8 — Hang it level: Use a spirit level. Always. Even pieces that look "nearly level" will bother you every day.
Pro Tip: If you are working with acrylic glazing rather than glass, remove the protective film only at the very last moment before assembly — static builds up on acrylic and attracts dust like a magnet.

How to Frame Canvas vs Paper vs Print Contemporary Art

Not all contemporary art is created equal when it comes to framing — the medium makes a real difference to the approach. Let me break this down by type because the rules genuinely vary.

Medium-by-Medium Framing Guide

  • Stretched canvas: No glazing needed. Use a floater frame — this sits around the canvas with a small gap so the edges of the painting remain visible. Choose a frame depth that matches your canvas depth (check this before buying). Canvas does not need a mount.
  • Unstretched / rolled canvas: Either stretch it yourself onto a wooden stretcher frame first, or take it to a professional framer. Do not frame it flat without stretching — it will wrinkle and sag.
  • Watercolour, gouache, or original on paper: Always use conservation-grade materials throughout. Hinge the artwork (do not dry-mount or glue it). Use UV-protective glazing. A generous mount helps protect the paper and creates a beautiful gallery feel.
  • Giclée or archival art print: Treat like paper — acid-free mount, UV glazing, hinge hanging. Avoid dry-mounting unless you do not mind it being permanent (dry-mounting bonds the print to a board and cannot be reversed).
  • Poster or non-archival print: Standard framing is fine here since archival longevity is less of a concern. A simple clip frame or standard frame with float glass works well.
  • Mixed media / textured pieces: Use a box frame or spacer bars to create depth between the artwork surface and the glazing. This protects raised elements and gives the piece room to be itself.

She had taken it to a cheap framing service that dry-mounted it — permanently bonded it to a backing board with no reversibility. If she had ever wanted to reframe it or sell it, the damage would have been irreversible. Always ask a framer whether they use reversible mounting methods for original art.

More About Getting Framing Right

Framing is genuinely one of those skills where a little knowledge goes a long way — and the gap between a competently framed piece and a poorly framed one is far more visible than most people expect.

One thing worth knowing is that the art world has thought carefully about this for a long time. If you want to go deeper on the theory side, this guide from Artsy — 5 Tips for Finding the Right Frame for Your Art — is a genuinely useful read from people who think about this professionally every day.

What I would add to the practical side is this: trust the artwork. Contemporary art is made by people who thought hard about colour, form and composition. Your job as the framer is to present it — not to interpret it or add to it.

When in doubt, go simpler. A plain, well-proportioned frame in a neutral colour will never embarrass you. It is the overcomplicated, over-matched, over-decorated frame that almost always dates and disappoints.

Have you ever stood in front of a blank wall, frames tucked under your arm, and suddenly had absolutely no idea where to start? I've been there — and so have almost every client I've worked with. The good news is that wall art arrangements that look effortlessly styled are almost always the result of careful planning, not happy accidents.

Quick answer: To plan a gallery wall layout, first gather your frames and trace them onto paper templates, then arrange those templates on the floor before taping them to the wall. Once you're happy with the arrangement, use the templates as hanging guides — marking nail positions through the paper — so every frame lands exactly where you want it.

Gallery wall layout planning is the process of deciding which frames go where, how much space sits between them, and how the overall shape of the arrangement fits your wall — before anything gets hung. Done well, it turns a random collection of pictures into something that feels cohesive and intentional. If you're looking for unique wall art to anchor your layout, or browsing for unique home decor to style the space around it, having a plan in place means you'll know exactly what sizes and styles to shop for.

How to Plan a Gallery Wall Layout Step by Step

The most reliable way to plan a gallery wall is to work through it in stages — choosing your wall, deciding your arrangement style, mapping it out flat, and then transferring it up. Rushing any of these steps is the main reason gallery walls end up lopsided or oddly spaced.

Here's the process I walk every client through, and honestly, it works every single time.

A woman of South Asian descent in her early 30s, wearing casual weekend clothes, kneeling on the floor and adjusting one of the paper templates with a thoughtful expression, measuring tape beside her, pencil tucked behind her ear.]]

Step-by-step gallery wall planning process

  • Step 1 — Choose your wall: Pick a wall with enough breathing room. A wall you see as soon as you enter a room is ideal — it becomes a natural focal point.
  • Step 2 — Decide your arrangement style: Grid (uniform, ordered), salon-style (loose, layered, mixed sizes), or symmetrical pairs. Pick one before you gather frames.
  • Step 3 — Gather everything you want to hang: Lay frames, prints, mirrors, and any other wall objects on the floor together so you can see what you're working with.
  • Step 4 — Arrange on the floor first: Shuffle pieces around until the overall shape, balance, and sizing feel right. Take a photo so you don't lose your arrangement.
  • Step 5 — Create paper templates: Trace each piece onto brown paper or newspaper, cut them out, and label each one on the back.
  • Step 6 — Tape templates to the wall: Use low-tack painter's tape to position your paper cut-outs exactly where you want each frame to hang.
  • Step 7 — Mark nail positions: Mark through the template where the hanging hardware sits, then remove the paper and hammer your nails or fix your picture hooks.
  • Step 8 — Hang and adjust: Hang each piece using your marks. Step back and make any small adjustments before you're done.
Pro Tip: Take a photo of your floor arrangement before you start cutting templates — it's your reference point if the paper gets shuffled around during taping.

Best Gallery Wall Arrangements and Spacing Tips

The arrangement style you choose sets the whole tone of the wall. A tight grid feels modern and structured; a salon-style arrangement feels collected and personal. Neither is wrong — it just depends on your room and your taste.

Spacing is where most people go a bit wrong, and it's an easy fix once you know the rule.

[[IMG|gallery-wall-arrangements-spacing-guide|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Gallery Wall Arrangements", then a clear VISUAL comparison showing three labelled layout types side by side: 1) Grid — uniform square frames in even rows; 2) Salon Style — mixed size frames arranged loosely; 3) Symmetrical — matching frames mirrored on either side of a centre point. Each layout type has a short label beneath it. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Popular arrangement styles and spacing rules

  • Grid layout: All frames the same size, hung in equal rows and columns. Keep spacing consistent at 5–8 cm between frames for a clean look.
  • Salon style: Mixed frame sizes arranged organically. Start with your largest piece slightly left or right of centre, then build outward.
  • Symmetrical layout: Pairs or sets of identical frames mirrored around a central piece — great over a fireplace or bed.
  • Linear / horizontal row: A single row of frames at the same height. Works brilliantly in hallways and along staircases.
  • Spacing between frames: 5–8 cm is the sweet spot for most arrangements. Too tight and it looks cluttered; too spread and it looks like separate pictures, not a wall.
  • Centre height: Aim for the visual centre of your arrangement to sit at approximately 145–150 cm from the floor — roughly eye level for most adults.
  • Above furniture: Leave roughly 20–25 cm of space between the top of the sofa, bed, or sideboard and the bottom of the lowest frame.

I once worked with a client who had spaced her frames nearly 20 cm apart because she was worried about them feeling too crowded. The wall ended up looking like six separate pictures rather than a gallery. We simply moved them all closer together, and the whole thing clicked into place — no new frames needed, no new nails, just tighter spacing.

Pro Tip: Cut a 6 cm strip of cardboard and use it as a physical spacer between frames as you hang them — far more accurate than trying to eyeball the gap.

How to Choose Frames and Art Sizes for a Gallery Wall

Frame and art size choices are what give a gallery wall its visual weight and rhythm. Too many small frames and the wall looks fussy; one frame too large and it dominates everything else. The aim is variety with a sense of balance.

A good rule of thumb I always share: aim for one or two "anchor" pieces (your largest frames), a handful of medium pieces, and a few smaller ones to fill gaps and add interest.

Frame and size selection guide

Frame role Recommended size How many to include Best for
Anchor piece 50 x 70 cm or larger 1–2 Setting the focal point; bold artwork or photography
Medium pieces 30 x 40 cm to 40 x 50 cm 3–5 Building the arrangement outward; prints, illustrations
Small accents 13 x 18 cm to 20 x 25 cm 2–4 Filling visual gaps; small photos, quotes, mini prints
Non-frame objects Varies 1–3 Mirrors, woven hangings, small shelves, wall sconces
  • Mix portrait and landscape orientations within the same arrangement for variety.
  • Keep frame colours consistent — or at least within a close family (all black, all natural wood, all white) — even if the art inside varies wildly.
  • Use mounts (mats) inside frames to make smaller art look more considered and gallery-like.
  • Don't size everything the same — identical sizes in a salon-style arrangement look flat and unconvincing.
Pro Tip: Lay all your potential frames on the floor against a plain surface and photograph them from above. Zoom out on the photo — if the arrangement looks good as a tiny thumbnail, it will look good on the wall.

How to Measure and Mark Your Wall Before Hanging

Measuring properly before you touch a hammer is what separates a gallery wall that looks professional from one that ends up slightly off-centre and hard to fix. It takes an extra 20 minutes and saves a lot of unnecessary holes.

I'll be honest — I skipped this step early in my career and spent an embarrassing amount of time filling holes with polyfilla in a client's rented flat. Never again.

[[IMG|measuring-and-marking-wall-gallery-layout|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A close-up scene of a clean light grey wall in a hallway, with several irregularly shaped brown paper templates taped to the wall at different heights using low-tack blue painter's tape, arranged in a loose gallery-wall formation. A pencil mark and small sticky note are visible on one of the templates. A woman of East Asian descent in her mid 40s, wearing a striped cotton top, standing to the side and pressing a retractable measuring tape between two of the paper templates, checking the gap between them carefully.]]

How to measure and mark accurately

  • Find the centre of your wall: Measure the total width and divide by two. Mark this point lightly in pencil — this is your anchor point for a symmetrical or centred layout.
  • Mark the eye-level height: Draw a faint horizontal pencil line at 145–150 cm from the floor across the area where your arrangement will sit.
  • Measure from furniture: If hanging above a sofa or console, measure up from the top of the furniture and mark your lowest frame position first.
  • Use a spirit level: Even if your eye says it's straight, always check with a spirit level. A 1 cm tilt reads as crooked across a large arrangement.
  • Mark the hanging point per frame: Once templates are taped up, feel through the paper for where the hanging wire or hook sits on each frame. Mark that exact spot on the wall through the template.
  • Number your templates: Label each paper template and the corresponding frame (1, 2, 3…) so you know which nail belongs to which piece when you remove the paper.
  • Check for cables and pipes: Use a cable detector before drilling or hammering into any wall you're not 100% sure about — particularly in older UK homes.
Real Example: On a client's project in a Victorian terrace, we found the walls were noticeably out of plumb — what looked level by eye was actually a few degrees off. A spirit level caught it straight away and saved us from hanging an entire arrangement at a very slight but visible tilt.

Tools and Templates to Plan Your Gallery Wall Layout

You don't need expensive software or apps to plan a gallery wall well. Some of the best layouts I've ever helped create were planned with brown paper, a pencil, and a roll of painter's tape. That said, there are a few tools that genuinely make the job easier.

[[IMG|tools-for-gallery-wall-layout-planning|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Gallery Wall Planning Toolkit". Then a clear labelled visual showing six essential tools as simple flat icons arranged in a grid: 1) Measuring tape, 2) Spirit level, 3) Painter's tape (low-tack), 4) Brown paper / newspaper, 5) Pencil and scissors, 6) Picture hooks / nails. Each icon has a short label beneath it. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Essential gallery wall planning tools

  • Retractable measuring tape: Non-negotiable. Measure twice, hang once.
  • Spirit level (or a level app): A small bubble level works perfectly. A digital level app on your phone is a decent backup.
  • Low-tack painter's tape: For sticking paper templates to the wall without damaging paint.
  • Brown parcel paper or newspaper: For creating your DIY templates (more on this below).
  • Pencil and scissors: Light pencil marks are easy to erase; scissors give clean template edges.
  • Picture hooks and a hammer (or adhesive strips): For rented or plastered walls, adhesive strips rated to the right weight are worth considering.
  • Cable/stud detector: Invaluable before drilling or hammering into unfamiliar walls.
  • Sticky notes: Write the frame name or number on a sticky note attached to each template so you know what belongs where.
Pro Tip: If you want to plan digitally first, a free tool like Canva lets you drag rectangles around to simulate frame arrangements — useful for experimenting with layouts before you cut a single template.

Printable or DIY Paper Template Method for Planning Without Software

The paper template method is genuinely the best way to plan a gallery wall layout, full stop. It's free, it's tactile, and it gives you a real-world preview of exactly how the arrangement will sit on your wall. I recommend it to every single person I work with, regardless of budget.

If you've never tried it, here's the full process broken down simply.

[[IMG|diy-paper-template-gallery-wall-method|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A cosy living room with a warm cream wall, multiple brown paper and newspaper cut-outs taped to the wall in a loose salon-style arrangement using strips of blue painter's tape, some templates labelled with handwritten numbers. A large wooden coffee table in the foreground has scissors, a pencil, leftover brown paper scraps, and a measuring tape on it. A man of South American descent in his late 20s, wearing a casual grey jumper, crouches in front of the wall adjusting the position of one of the lower paper templates, checking it with a small spirit level.]]

How to make and use DIY paper templates

  • Trace your frames: Lay each frame face-down on brown paper or newspaper. Draw around the outer edge with a pencil, then cut it out neatly.
  • Mark the hanging point: While the frame is still face-down, find where the wire or hook would actually sit if it were on the wall — mark this clearly on your paper template (it's usually 3–8 cm down from the top, depending on the frame).
  • Label each template: Write the frame name, size, and orientation on the paper with a marker so you don't mix them up.
  • Arrange on the floor first: Lay all templates out on the floor in your chosen arrangement. Shuffle them freely — this step costs nothing, so experiment.
  • Tape to the wall: Once you're happy with the floor arrangement, transfer the templates to the wall using low-tack painter's tape. Take your time repositioning until it looks right.
  • Step back and assess: Walk to the opposite end of the room and look at the arrangement from a distance. Adjust any templates that feel off.
  • Mark nail positions: Once confirmed, press a pencil through the hanging-point mark on each template to transfer the nail position to the wall. Remove templates and hang your frames using those marks.

A client of mine was convinced she needed a digital planning app to get her layout right. I posted her a roll of brown paper and told her to just trace her frames and stick them up. She sent me a photo two hours later — the layout was perfect, and she hadn't downloaded a single thing.

Pro Tip: If you want a printable grid template, simply draw your wall dimensions to scale on graph paper, using one square to represent 10 cm. You can then sketch in your frame rectangles to scale before committing to templates.

Room-by-Room Gallery Wall Layout Ideas

Different rooms call for different gallery wall approaches. What works beautifully in a living room might feel overwhelming in a narrow hallway, and what's perfect for a bedroom might look too casual in a formal dining space. Here's how I think about each room differently.

Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). A family scene with a woman and her young daughter of mixed heritage, the child holding a paper cut-out template up to the hallway wall playfully while the mother smiles and watches.]]

Gallery wall ideas by room

  • Living room: This is the most forgiving space for a gallery wall. A large salon-style arrangement above the sofa works brilliantly — mix sizes freely, use a large anchor print, and bring in one or two non-frame elements like a small mirror or a woven hanging. Aim for the arrangement to be roughly two-thirds the width of the sofa beneath it.
  • Bedroom: Above the bed is the classic spot. Keep it calmer and more curated than a living room wall — symmetrical layouts or pairs work well here. Stick to a softer colour palette to keep the room restful.
  • Hallway: Work with the narrow, vertical space. A linear horizontal row at eye level runs beautifully along a hallway. Alternatively, a staircase gallery wall going diagonally upward is a classic and very effective use of an awkward space.
  • Dining room: A more formal symmetrical arrangement suits the more structured nature of dining spaces. Botanical prints, abstract art, or a collection of vintage-style illustrations work well here.
  • Home office / study: Use a smaller, tighter arrangement — something focused and contained rather than sprawling. A 3 x 3 grid of prints or a collection of meaningful personal photos keeps the space motivating without being distracting.
  • Children's room: Keep frames lightweight, use adhesive hooks rated to the correct weight, and choose fun, colourful artwork. Leave room to swap pieces in and out as the child grows.
Real Example: I worked on a narrow Victorian hallway that was less than 90 cm wide. Instead of a traditional gallery wall, we did a single diagonal line of small matching frames following the staircase — seven frames, all in the same black border, alternating portrait and landscape. It looked far more considered than a crowded multi-frame arrangement would have in that tight space.

Common Gallery Wall Layout Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

I've seen gallery walls go sideways (sometimes literally) for very predictable reasons. The mistakes tend to cluster around the same few issues — and all of them are avoidable once you know what to look for.

Here are the ones I see most often, and exactly how to fix each one.

[[IMG|common-gallery-wall-mistakes-avoid|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Common Gallery Wall Mistakes". Then a VISUAL comparison showing five labelled mistake icons on the left side and their corresponding fix icons on the right side, arranged in a vertical list with a clear dividing line: 1) Frames too spread apart → close to 5–8cm spacing; 2) All same size frames → mix anchor + medium + small; 3) No planning on floor first → arrange on floor before hanging; 4) Arrangement hung too high → centre at 145cm from floor; 5) Mixed frame colours without intention → unify frame finish. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Mistakes to avoid and how to fix them

  • Hanging too high: The single most common mistake. People instinctively hang things at head height, but gallery walls look best when the visual centre is at roughly 145–150 cm from the floor — lower than you think.
  • All the same frame size: Even in a grid, matching sizes can look flat if the art inside isn't varied. In a salon-style arrangement, identical sizes kill the organic feel entirely.
  • Frames too far apart: Spacing larger than 10 cm and the arrangement stops reading as a gallery wall — it just looks like separate pictures. Keep gaps at 5–8 cm.
  • Not planning before hanging: Skipping the floor-arrangement or paper-template stage is the biggest source of extra holes and frustration. Always plan first.
  • Using too many competing colours in frames: A mix of gold, silver, black, and wood all in one arrangement rarely works. Choose one or two finishes and stick to them.
  • Ignoring the wall space around the arrangement: A gallery wall needs breathing room. Leave enough plain wall on all sides — don't cram it into a corner or let it run to the ceiling.
  • Hanging without checking for level: Even one frame that's slightly tilted will pull the eye and make the whole arrangement feel off.
Pro Tip: Before you commit to a nail, hold each frame up in position and take a photo on your phone. View the photos back-to-back to get a clearer sense of how the arrangement will look when all pieces are hung together.

How to Mix Art Styles, Frames, and Mediums Cohesively

A gallery wall that mixes photography with illustration, or oil painting with watercolour, can look brilliant — but it can also look chaotic if there's no thread holding it together. The secret isn't to match everything; it's to find a unifying element that ties different pieces into a whole.

Think of it like styling an outfit: you can mix prints and textures, but something — a colour, a material, a silhouette — has to connect it all.

[[IMG|mixing-art-styles-frames-mediums-gallery-wall|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls (the store's real wall art is shown separately through product images). Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. A styled flat-lay on a wide light oak dining table showing an eclectic collection of decorative objects that represent different art mediums and textures: a small ceramic vase, a woven textile swatch, a terracotta pot with a trailing plant, a stack of design books with colour-blocked spines, and some paper colour swatches in muted tones — dusty rose, sage green, warm sand, charcoal. A woman of Eastern European descent in her early 50s, wearing a relaxed linen blazer, sits at the table studying the colour swatches and comparing two of them side by side, surrounded by the objects.]]

How to create cohesion across mixed styles

  • Unify through colour palette: Even if every piece of art is completely different in subject and style, a consistent colour palette (say, all dusty tones, or all monochromes) makes everything feel intentional.
  • Use a consistent frame finish: All-black frames, all natural timber, or all white frames will hold together even the most eclectic collection of art.
  • Mix mediums intentionally: Photography, illustration, watercolour, and textile art can all share a wall happily — but aim for no more than three different mediums in one arrangement to avoid visual noise.
  • Repeat a motif or subject: If several pieces share a theme — botanicals, architecture, figures, abstract shapes — it creates cohesion even when styles differ.
  • Balance visual weight: A very bold, dark piece needs lighter pieces around it to balance. A wall of all-similar-weight pieces looks flat. Vary the density intentionally.
  • Include one non-frame element: A small mirror, a macramé hanging, or a ceramic wall sculpture breaks the visual repetition of frames and adds dimension and texture.
  • Don't overthink it: If pieces genuinely mean something to you — photos from travels, art you love, gifts from people you care about — that personal connection usually gives the arrangement its own coherence naturally.

I helped a client who had inherited several very traditional oil-painting-style prints alongside a collection of modern line-art drawings she'd bought herself. We tied them together with deep forest-green frames throughout and kept the wall palette neutral. The mix of old and new actually became the talking point of the room rather than looking like a mismatch.

Pro Tip: When in doubt, lay all your potential pieces on the bed or floor and photograph them together from above. If the overall image looks harmonious as a flat lay, it will work on the wall.

More About Gallery Wall Layout Planning: What the Experts Say

Good gallery wall layout planning is backed up by a surprisingly consistent set of principles — and interior design experts tend to agree on the fundamentals, even when their styles differ.

One principle that comes up again and again is the idea of starting with your largest piece and building outward, rather than trying to plan the whole arrangement from scratch. It gives you a stable anchor point and makes the rest of the decisions easier. This approach is well supported by the detailed walkthrough in How To Actually Make A Gallery Wall: Our No-Fail Formula We Use Every Time (+ Our Favourite Original Art Resources), which breaks down a tested process that professional stylists use on real shoots and real homes. Ready to Start Your Gallery Wall? Here's Where to Begin

Gallery wall layout planning really does come down to one thing: doing the groundwork before anything touches a nail. Measure your wall, gather your pieces, get them on the floor, and make your templates — and you'll find the whole process far less daunting than it looks from the outside.

You don't need perfect frames, a designer budget, or years of experience. You need a roll of brown paper, a spirit level, and a clear idea of what you love. The rest follows from there.

If you're still in the early stages of collecting pieces, start with one or two things you genuinely love and build from there — a gallery wall is always a living thing that can grow and change over time. It doesn't have to be finished on day one.

Quick answer: To plan a gallery wall layout, first gather your frames and trace them onto paper templates, then arrange those templates on the floor before taping them to the wall. Once you're happy with the arrangement, use the templates as hanging guides — marking nail positions through the paper — so every frame lands exactly where you want it.

Gallery wall layout planning is the process of deciding which frames go where, how much space sits between them, and how the overall shape of the arrangement fits your wall — before anything gets hung. Done well, it turns a random collection of pictures into something that feels cohesive and intentional. How to Plan a Gallery Wall Layout Step by Step

The most reliable way to plan a gallery wall is to work through it in stages — choosing your wall, deciding your arrangement style, mapping it out flat, and then transferring it up. Rushing any of these steps is the main reason gallery walls end up lopsided or oddly spaced.

Here's the process I walk every client through, and honestly, it works every single time.

Step-by-step gallery wall planning process

  • Step 1 — Choose your wall: Pick a wall with enough breathing room. A wall you see as soon as you enter a room is ideal — it becomes a natural focal point.
  • Step 2 — Decide your arrangement style: Grid (uniform, ordered), salon-style (loose, layered, mixed sizes), or symmetrical pairs. Pick one before you gather frames.
  • Step 3 — Gather everything you want to hang: Lay frames, prints, mirrors, and any other wall objects on the floor together so you can see what you're working with.
  • Step 4 — Arrange on the floor first: Shuffle pieces around until the overall shape, balance, and sizing feel right. Take a photo so you don't lose your arrangement.
  • Step 5 — Create paper templates: Trace each piece onto brown paper or newspaper, cut them out, and label each one on the back.
  • Step 6 — Tape templates to the wall: Use low-tack painter's tape to position your paper cut-outs exactly where you want each frame to hang.
  • Step 7 — Mark nail positions: Mark through the template where the hanging hardware sits, then remove the paper and hammer your nails or fix your picture hooks.
  • Step 8 — Hang and adjust: Hang each piece using your marks. Step back and make any small adjustments before you're done.
Pro Tip: Take a photo of your floor arrangement before you start cutting templates — it's your reference point if the paper gets shuffled around during taping.

Best Gallery Wall Arrangements and Spacing Tips

The arrangement style you choose sets the whole tone of the wall. A tight grid feels modern and structured; a salon-style arrangement feels collected and personal. Neither is wrong — it just depends on your room and your taste.

Spacing is where most people go a bit wrong, and it's an easy fix once you know the rule.

Popular arrangement styles and spacing rules

  • Grid layout: All frames the same size, hung in equal rows and columns. Keep spacing consistent at 5–8 cm between frames for a clean look.
  • Salon style: Mixed frame sizes arranged organically. Start with your largest piece slightly left or right of centre, then build outward.
  • Symmetrical layout: Pairs or sets of identical frames mirrored around a central piece — great over a fireplace or bed.
  • Linear / horizontal row: A single row of frames at the same height. Works brilliantly in hallways and along staircases.
  • Spacing between frames: 5–8 cm is the sweet spot for most arrangements. Too tight and it looks cluttered; too spread and it looks like separate pictures, not a wall.
  • Centre height: Aim for the visual centre of your arrangement to sit at approximately 145–150 cm from the floor — roughly eye level for most adults.
  • Above furniture: Leave roughly 20–25 cm of space between the top of the sofa, bed, or sideboard and the bottom of the lowest frame.

I once worked with a client who had spaced her frames nearly 20 cm apart because she was worried about them feeling too crowded. The wall ended up looking like six separate pictures rather than a gallery. We simply moved them all closer together, and the whole thing clicked into place — no new frames needed, no new nails, just tighter spacing.

Pro Tip: Cut a 6 cm strip of cardboard and use it as a physical spacer between frames as you hang them — far more accurate than trying to eyeball the gap.

How to Choose Frames and Art Sizes for a Gallery Wall

Frame and art size choices are what give a gallery wall its visual weight and rhythm. Too many small frames and the wall looks fussy; one frame too large and it dominates everything else. The aim is variety with a sense of balance.

A good rule of thumb I always share: aim for one or two "anchor" pieces (your largest frames), a handful of medium pieces, and a few smaller ones to fill gaps and add interest.

  • Mix portrait and landscape orientations within the same arrangement for variety.
  • Keep frame colours consistent — or at least within a close family (all black, all natural wood, all white) — even if the art inside varies wildly.
  • Use mounts (mats) inside frames to make smaller art look more considered and gallery-like.
  • Don't size everything the same — identical sizes in a salon-style arrangement look flat and unconvincing.

How to Measure and Mark Your Wall Before Hanging

Measuring properly before you touch a hammer is what separates a gallery wall that looks professional from one that ends up slightly off-centre and hard to fix. It takes an extra 20 minutes and saves a lot of unnecessary holes.

I'll be honest — I skipped this step early in my career and spent an embarrassing amount of time filling holes with polyfilla in a client's rented flat. Never again.

How to measure and mark accurately

  • Find the centre of your wall: Measure the total width and divide by two. Mark this point lightly in pencil — this is your anchor point for a symmetrical or centred layout.
  • Mark the eye-level height: Draw a faint horizontal pencil line at 145–150 cm from the floor across the area where your arrangement will sit.
  • Measure from furniture: If hanging above a sofa or console, measure up from the top of the furniture and mark your lowest frame position first.
  • Use a spirit level: Even if your eye says it's straight, always check with a spirit level. A 1 cm tilt reads as crooked across a large arrangement.
  • Mark the hanging point per frame: Once templates are taped up, feel through the paper for where the hanging wire or hook sits on each frame. Mark that exact spot on the wall through the template.
  • Number your templates: Label each paper template and the corresponding frame (1, 2, 3…) so you know which nail belongs to which piece when you remove the paper.
  • Check for cables and pipes: Use a cable detector before drilling or hammering into any wall you're not 100% sure about — particularly in older UK homes.
Real Example: On a client's project in a Victorian terrace, we found the walls were noticeably out of plumb — what looked level by eye was actually a few degrees off. A spirit level caught it straight away and saved us from hanging an entire arrangement at a very slight but visible tilt.

Tools and Templates to Plan Your Gallery Wall Layout

You don't need expensive software or apps to plan a gallery wall well. Some of the best layouts I've ever helped create were planned with brown paper, a pencil, and a roll of painter's tape. That said, there are a few tools that genuinely make the job easier.

Essential gallery wall planning tools

  • Retractable measuring tape: Non-negotiable. Measure twice, hang once.
  • Spirit level (or a level app): A small bubble level works perfectly. A digital level app on your phone is a decent backup.
  • Low-tack painter's tape: For sticking paper templates to the wall without damaging paint.
  • Brown parcel paper or newspaper: For creating your DIY templates (more on this below).
  • Pencil and scissors: Light pencil marks are easy to erase; scissors give clean template edges.
  • Picture hooks and a hammer (or adhesive strips): For rented or plastered walls, adhesive strips rated to the right weight are worth considering.
  • Cable/stud detector: Invaluable before drilling or hammering into unfamiliar walls.
  • Sticky notes: Write the frame name or number on a sticky note attached to each template so you know what belongs where.
Pro Tip: If you want to plan digitally first, a free tool like Canva lets you drag rectangles around to simulate frame arrangements — useful for experimenting with layouts before you cut a single template.

Printable or DIY Paper Template Method for Planning Without Software

The paper template method is genuinely the best way to plan a gallery wall layout, full stop. It's free, it's tactile, and it gives you a real-world preview of exactly how the arrangement will sit on your wall. I recommend it to every single person I work with, regardless of budget.

If you've never tried it, here's the full process broken down simply.

How to make and use DIY paper templates

  • Trace your frames: Lay each frame face-down on brown paper or newspaper. Draw around the outer edge with a pencil, then cut it out neatly.
  • Mark the hanging point: While the frame is still face-down, find where the wire or hook would actually sit if it were on the wall — mark this clearly on your paper template (it's usually 3–8 cm down from the top, depending on the frame).
  • Label each template: Write the frame name, size, and orientation on the paper with a marker so you don't mix them up.
  • Arrange on the floor first: Lay all templates out on the floor in your chosen arrangement. Shuffle them freely — this step costs nothing, so experiment.
  • Tape to the wall: Once you're happy with the floor arrangement, transfer the templates to the wall using low-tack painter's tape. Take your time repositioning until it looks right.
  • Step back and assess: Walk to the opposite end of the room and look at the arrangement from a distance. Adjust any templates that feel off.
  • Mark nail positions: Once confirmed, press a pencil through the hanging-point mark on each template to transfer the nail position to the wall. Remove templates and hang your frames using those marks.

A client of mine was convinced she needed a digital planning app to get her layout right. I posted her a roll of brown paper and told her to just trace her frames and stick them up. She sent me a photo two hours later — the layout was perfect, and she hadn't downloaded a single thing.

Pro Tip: If you want a printable grid template, simply draw your wall dimensions to scale on graph paper, using one square to represent 10 cm. You can then sketch in your frame rectangles to scale before committing to templates.

Room-by-Room Gallery Wall Layout Ideas

Different rooms call for different gallery wall approaches. What works beautifully in a living room might feel overwhelming in a narrow hallway, and what's perfect for a bedroom might look too casual in a formal dining space. Here's how I think about each room differently.

Gallery wall ideas by room

  • Living room: This is the most forgiving space for a gallery wall. A large salon-style arrangement above the sofa works brilliantly — mix sizes freely, use a large anchor print, and bring in one or two non-frame elements like a small mirror or a woven hanging. Aim for the arrangement to be roughly two-thirds the width of the sofa beneath it.
  • Bedroom: Above the bed is the classic spot. Keep it calmer and more curated than a living room wall — symmetrical layouts or pairs work well here. Stick to a softer colour palette to keep the room restful.
  • Hallway: Work with the narrow, vertical space. A linear horizontal row at eye level runs beautifully along a hallway. Alternatively, a staircase gallery wall going diagonally upward is a classic and very effective use of an awkward space.
  • Dining room: A more formal symmetrical arrangement suits the more structured nature of dining spaces. Botanical prints, abstract art, or a collection of vintage-style illustrations work well here.
  • Home office / study: Use a smaller, tighter arrangement — something focused and contained rather than sprawling. A 3 x 3 grid of prints or a collection of meaningful personal photos keeps the space motivating without being distracting.
  • Children's room: Keep frames lightweight, use adhesive hooks rated to the correct weight, and choose fun, colourful artwork. Leave room to swap pieces in and out as the child grows.
Real Example: I worked on a narrow Victorian hallway that was less than 90 cm wide. Instead of a traditional gallery wall, we did a single diagonal line of small matching frames following the staircase — seven frames, all in the same black border, alternating portrait and landscape. It looked far more considered than a crowded multi-frame arrangement would have in that tight space.

Common Gallery Wall Layout Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

I've seen gallery walls go sideways (sometimes literally) for very predictable reasons. The mistakes tend to cluster around the same few issues — and all of them are avoidable once you know what to look for.

Here are the ones I see most often, and exactly how to fix each one.

Mistakes to avoid and how to fix them

  • Hanging too high: The single most common mistake. People instinctively hang things at head height, but gallery walls look best when the visual centre is at roughly 145–150 cm from the floor — lower than you think.
  • All the same frame size: Even in a grid, matching sizes can look flat if the art inside isn't varied. In a salon-style arrangement, identical sizes kill the organic feel entirely.
  • Frames too far apart: Spacing larger than 10 cm and the arrangement stops reading as a gallery wall — it just looks like separate pictures. Keep gaps at 5–8 cm.
  • Not planning before hanging: Skipping the floor-arrangement or paper-template stage is the biggest source of extra holes and frustration. Always plan first.
  • Using too many competing colours in frames: A mix of gold, silver, black, and wood all in one arrangement rarely works. Choose one or two finishes and stick to them.
  • Ignoring the wall space around the arrangement: A gallery wall needs breathing room. Leave enough plain wall on all sides — don't cram it into a corner or let it run to the ceiling.
  • Hanging without checking for level: Even one frame that's slightly tilted will pull the eye and make the whole arrangement feel off.
Pro Tip: Before you commit to a nail, hold each frame up in position and take a photo on your phone. View the photos back-to-back to get a clearer sense of how the arrangement will look when all pieces are hung together.

How to Mix Art Styles, Frames, and Mediums Cohesively

A gallery wall that mixes photography with illustration, or oil painting with watercolour, can look brilliant — but it can also look chaotic if there's no thread holding it together. The secret isn't to match everything; it's to find a unifying element that ties different pieces into a whole.

Think of it like styling an outfit: you can mix prints and textures, but something — a colour, a material, a silhouette — has to connect it all.

How to create cohesion across mixed styles

  • Unify through colour palette: Even if every piece of art is completely different in subject and style, a consistent colour palette (say, all dusty tones, or all monochromes) makes everything feel intentional.
  • Use a consistent frame finish: All-black frames, all natural timber, or all white frames will hold together even the most eclectic collection of art.
  • Mix mediums intentionally: Photography, illustration, watercolour, and textile art can all share a wall happily — but aim for no more than three different mediums in one arrangement to avoid visual noise.
  • Repeat a motif or subject: If several pieces share a theme — botanicals, architecture, figures, abstract shapes — it creates cohesion even when styles differ.
  • Balance visual weight: A very bold, dark piece needs lighter pieces around it to balance. A wall of all-similar-weight pieces looks flat. Vary the density intentionally.
  • Include one non-frame element: A small mirror, a macramé hanging, or a ceramic wall sculpture breaks the visual repetition of frames and adds dimension and texture.
  • Don't overthink it: If pieces genuinely mean something to you — photos from travels, art you love, gifts from people you care about — that personal connection usually gives the arrangement its own coherence naturally.

I helped a client who had inherited several very traditional oil-painting-style prints alongside a collection of modern line-art drawings she'd bought herself. We tied them together with deep forest-green frames throughout and kept the wall palette neutral. The mix of old and new actually became the talking point of the room rather than looking like a mismatch.

Pro Tip: When in doubt, lay all your potential pieces on the bed or floor and photograph them together from above. If the overall image looks harmonious as a flat lay, it will work on the wall.

Art Types Matched to Bedroom Moods

  • Calm and restful: Soft watercolours, nature-inspired botanical prints, misty landscape photography in muted tones
  • Romantic and intimate: Abstract art with warm terracotta, blush or gold tones; soft figurative line art
  • Bold and energised: Geometric prints, graphic typography, high-contrast black and white photography
  • Cosy and earthy: Textured woven wall hangings, folk art, hand-drawn maps or illustrated botanical studies
  • Luxurious and refined: Monochrome fine art prints in wide mats with slim frames, architectural photography
  • Playful and creative: Mixed media, collage-style prints, colourful abstract expressionism

Real Example: A couple I worked with couldn't agree on art — she wanted something serene, he wanted something with a bit of punch. We compromised with a large-scale botanical print in deep forest green: calm enough to wind down to, but rich and graphic enough to feel interesting. Both were completely happy, and it's now the focal point of their entire room.

How to Hang and Position Bedroom Wall Art Like a Pro

Hanging art correctly is genuinely a skill, and getting it right transforms a room in a way that's hard to explain until you've seen it. The single most important rule? Eye level — and I mean actual eye level, not "roughly centre of the wall."

The professional standard is to hang the centre of the artwork at approximately 145 to 152 cm from the floor. This is the average standing eye level and it's used by galleries and designers universally. When art hangs too high (which is the most common mistake), it disconnects from the furniture and looks like it's floating.

[[IMG|how-to-hang-bedroom-wall-art-positioning|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — a macramé hanging, wall-mounted sconce lighting, a decorative shelf. A Black British woman in her late 30s stands on the left side of the bed, holding a tape measure to the wall at about chest height, looking up with a focused, practical expression — casual daytime clothing.]]

Step-by-Step: Hanging Art Like a Pro

  • Mark the centre point — measure and lightly mark 148 cm from the floor with a pencil. This is where the centre of your artwork should sit.
  • Account for the hanging hardware — measure from the top of the frame to where the wire or hook sits, then subtract that from the height of the artwork centre to find your nail point.
  • Use a spirit level — even a small angle is visible and it will drive you mad. Never hang anything without checking.
  • For above-the-bed placement — leave 15 to 20 cm of space between the top of the headboard and the bottom of the artwork. Closer than that looks cluttered; further than that looks disconnected.
  • Two hooks for large pieces — anything wider than 60 cm should have two hooks spaced evenly to prevent tilting over time.
  • Test with paper first — tape the cut-out to the wall at the exact position before committing any nails.
Pro Tip: If you're renting and can't put nails in the wall, adhesive strips rated for your artwork's weight are a genuine option — just make sure the weight is within the product's rating. Always err on the side of caution and go heavier-rated than you think you need.

Step-by-Step Pro Tips for Measuring and Planning a Gallery Wall in a Bedroom

A gallery wall is one of the most impactful things you can do in a bedroom — but it requires proper planning, or it becomes a chaotic mess of mismatched frames. I've seen both outcomes, and the difference is almost always about whether someone did the prep work first.

The professional method is simple: plan everything on paper (or on the floor) before you touch a single wall. It takes an extra thirty minutes and saves you hours of filling holes and repainting.

Each step has a two-word label underneath. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Gallery Wall Planning: Step by Step

  • Step 1 — Choose your focal anchor piece first. This is usually the largest or most important item in the grouping. Everything else builds around it.
  • Step 2 — Lay all pieces on the floor. Arrange them until you're happy, then photograph the layout. This is your reference.
  • Step 3 — Trace each frame onto paper and cut them out. Label each one on the back.
  • Step 4 — Tape the paper cut-outs to the wall with painter's tape. Step back, adjust, live with it for a few hours.
  • Step 5 — Mark your nail points through the paper before removing each template. Remove the paper, nail in place.
  • Step 6 — Maintain consistent gaps. 5 to 8 cm between frames. Set a cardboard spacer to the right width and use it throughout.
  • Step 7 — Mix frame widths but stick to one finish. Mixing thin and chunky frames in all black, for example, creates cohesion without uniformity.

Here's what happened when I planned a gallery wall for myself at home without doing the floor layout step first — I was in a hurry and thought I had a good enough eye for it. Twenty minutes later I had four holes in the wrong place and a wall that looked genuinely unhinged. I ended up doing it properly the second time and it took half as long. The prep really is the work.

Pro Tip: Use a mix of at least three different frame sizes in a gallery wall — small, medium, and large — to create visual rhythm. All-same-size groupings can look a bit flat and corporate, which is rarely the vibe you want in a bedroom.
